title: Ai Adoption: Practice Exam
description: Timed practice exam covering the whole series. Pass with 72% or higher to earn the course completion certificate.

questions.question: A team asks to add a second design tool to the stack because it generates better images for their specific work. Under Lesson 31's front-door controls, what has to be true for that request to proceed?
options: The tool must be free, since free tools do not count against the stack
The team must wait for the annual audit before any new tool can be considered
Another tool leaves the stack, or the requester shows the new tool does a job the primary cannot, with a named owner and a review date recorded as an exception
The department head must approve it, and approval alone is sufficient to add it
questions.explanation: Lesson 31 sets out a one-in, one-out rule for new tools in an existing category: a tool enters only when another leaves or the requester shows it does a job the primary cannot. Exceptions are allowed, but the four-sentence test requires naming the specific job, the team, the capability the primary lacks, and a review date. Free tools are not exempt, and departmental approval alone is drift rather than a decision with an expiry.

questions.question: Priya scales her support automation and wants the monthly review to actually decide something. Which practice from Lesson 29 makes the review a real decision mechanism rather than theater?
options: Rotating the review criteria each month so the conversation stays fresh
Naming the gate decision in advance, keeping a single shared evidence pack that tracks benefits and total cost of ownership, and using the same evidence for both finance and the AI program
Reviewing only the use cases that are clearly succeeding and skipping the rest
Letting the vendor present its own success metrics at each review
questions.explanation: The lesson says gates only work when the decision criteria are named before the project starts and the evidence pack is single and shared, so the gate meeting decides instead of becoming a dispute about data. Running AI as a managed investment means a fixed review cadence, clear stage gates, and one evidence pack that tracks both benefits and total cost of ownership.

questions.question: A finance director approves seats for every employee who is technically eligible, on an annual commitment, so that nobody is blocked on day one. Based on Lesson 32, what has that decision removed?
options: Nothing important, because full coverage is the end state any rollout is aiming for
The waitlist, which is a measurement of declared intent, and the ability to shrink the count mid-term, since adding seats later is a phone call while removing them is a negotiation
The need to provision accounts through the identity provider, because bulk assignment replaces group-based provisioning
The requirement to measure adoption, because a fully licensed population is the same as a fully adopted one
questions.explanation: Lesson 32 separates eligibility from adoption and argues you should almost never buy to the eligible population at the start. Buying to eligibility converts a behavior question into a sunk cost and removes the waitlist, which tells you which teams are pulling. It also conflicts with the contract asymmetry the lesson calls the single most important fact: adding seats mid-term is usually easy, removing them is not, so the purchased count holds until renewal.

questions.question: Lesson 16 uses the four-level data classification model. Which pair of data types maps correctly to the Confidential and Restricted levels, respectively?
options: Confidential: employee handbooks. Restricted: marketing materials.
Confidential: customer records, contracts, and financial records. Restricted: trade secrets, source code, and active M&A documents.
Confidential: press releases. Restricted: standard operating procedures.
Confidential and Restricted are the same level and mean public information
questions.explanation: Lesson 16 defines Confidential as customer records, employee personal information, contracts, financial records, legal documents, partner agreements, and sensitive business plans. Restricted is the most sensitive tier: trade secrets, source code, intellectual property, board materials, active M&A documents, and regulated personal information.

questions.question: Why does the lesson insist you pair the north-star metric with a guardrail metric rather than tracking only the north-star?
options: Because without a second number you cannot calculate a percentage
Because the north-star metric is unreliable and needs a backup for accuracy
Because a single metric can be met by harming quality, and the guardrail catches the cheap way when the measured improvement is not real
Because stakeholders always want to see more than one chart
questions.explanation: The lesson grounds the guardrail in Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target it stops being a good measure, because people chase the number the cheap way. A guardrail metric, such as the reviewer-correction rate, is the early warning that the north-star is being met by cutting quality.

questions.question: In the worked example, the firm's customer-facing assistant produced a wrong billing reply that a human sent without checking. What was the firm's actual failure, according to Lesson 22?
options: The assistant was fundamentally broken and should never have been deployed
The firm had no detection signal for a wrong answer a human did not catch, and no real review step for billing-related replies
The customer should not have complained to the consumer protection agency
The firm should have banned the assistant entirely after the first mistake
questions.explanation: The lesson concludes that the firm's failure was not the assistant, which was always going to be wrong sometimes, but the absence of detection and the absence of a real review step. A sample review of sent replies or a second check on billing replies would have caught it.

questions.question: Lesson 1 defines the relationship between a rollout and a running program. Which describes it correctly?
options: A rollout is the ongoing work of sustaining adoption, while a program is the one-time launch effort
A rollout is a bounded effort with a timeline and an end, while a running program is ongoing work with no finish line
A rollout and a running program are the same thing under different names
A running program is a single training session, while a rollout manages usage over time
questions.explanation: Lesson 1 defines rollout as a bounded effort with a goal, steps, timeline, and end, and a running program as the ongoing work of sustaining adoption, measuring value, and governing use, with no finish line. AI adoption is a program, not a project.

questions.question: Lesson 22 presents a six-step response sequence. What is the correct order a non-technical owner should follow when an AI tool goes wrong?
options: Investigate, remediate, detect, contain, report, learn
Detect, contain, investigate, remediate, report, learn
Report, detect, contain, learn, investigate, remediate
Contain, report, detect, remediate, investigate, learn
questions.explanation: The lesson presents the sequence as detect, contain, investigate, remediate, report, learn. You detect the incident, contain the harm to stop it spreading, investigate the root cause, remediate the root cause, report to the people who need to know, and learn through a post-incident review.

questions.question: McKinsey's survey found C-suite leaders estimated only 4 percent of employees use gen AI for at least 30 percent of their daily work, while 13 percent of employees reported doing so. Why does this perception gap matter for an adoption program?
options: It confirms that leadership's estimates are accurate enough to plan from
Because you cannot govern, measure, or scale AI use you do not know exists, so a baseline built on leadership belief rather than ground truth will mis-set every downstream goal
It only matters for marketing purposes and has no effect on goals or budget
It shows the program should focus on the sanctioned pilot and ignore everything else
questions.explanation: The lesson argues the whole point of the audit is to replace leadership belief with ground truth. A baseline built on a guess will mis-set goals, budget, policy, and incident response, because you cannot govern or measure what you cannot see.

questions.question: In the worked example, why could the consulting firm not protect its flagship offer documents, and how did the data side fail?
options: The documents were too long to register, and the vendor refused to train on the data

The writers accepted most of the machine's expression and edited only lightly, so the outputs lacked protectable human authorship, and the firm had not read a data-use clause that allowed the vendor to use its data in aggregated or de-identified form for model training
The firm used a free tool, and free tools never hold copyright
The documents were all generated by a contractor rather than an employee
questions.explanation: Because the writers pasted most of the machine's expression and edited only lightly, the traditional elements of expression were determined by the AI, not the writers, so the outputs were largely unprotectable. On the data side, the firm signed a standard self-serve agreement without reading a data-use clause that let the vendor use customer data, inputs, outputs, and usage information in aggregated or de-identified form to improve models, putting confidential strategy and pricing into training.

questions.question: In the worked example, Priya books about 192,000 dollars of realized benefit rather than the 384,000 dollar headline saving. Why does the lesson endorse this?
options: Because the headline saving includes licence costs that should be subtracted twice
Because finance always discounts any claim by exactly half

Because she only counts the share of saved time that became realized value, an avoided new hire and higher-quality responses, and leaves the quarter that was not actually redeployed as on-paper upside
Because she is required to underreport results until the pilot runs for a full year
questions.explanation: Lesson 28 applies the redeemed-capacity test: a saving is only realized when the freed time becomes revenue, avoided cost, or reduced risk. Priya traced where the saved time went, booked the realized half (avoided hire and higher quality) as the hard number, and logged the unredeployed quarter as upside, because counting time saved that was never reinvested is a common way a claim collapses.

questions.question: According to Lesson 23, what is the difference between dependency and lock-in?
options: Dependency and lock-in are the same condition and the terms are interchangeable
Dependency means you need the thing, while lock-in means you cannot leave it without paying a cost you did not budget for
Lock-in means you need the thing, while dependency means you cannot leave it
Dependency only applies to the model, while lock-in only applies to the provider
questions.explanation: The lesson holds the framing from the start: dependency and lock-in are two different claims. Dependency means you need the thing. Lock-in means you cannot leave it, not without paying a price you did not budget for. Most organizations discover they were locked in only when they try to leave.

questions.question: According to the McKinsey survey cited in Lesson 2, where do cost benefits from AI use most commonly concentrate?
options: Uniformly across every business function in the enterprise
In software engineering, manufacturing, and IT
Mostly in marketing and sales, with little elsewhere
In no single function, because the survey found no cost benefits
questions.explanation: Lesson 2 reports that McKinsey's survey found cost benefits from AI concentrate in software engineering, manufacturing, and IT, all high-volume, predictable-input, cheap-to-verify work. Revenue increases are most often reported in marketing and sales, strategy and corporate finance, and product and service development.

questions.question: Lesson 3 describes the Boston Consulting Group field experiment and warns about the quality trap. What is the core warning about measuring speed without measuring quality?
options: On tasks inside the AI's capability frontier, people produced higher quality results, but on tasks outside it they were less likely to reach the correct solution, so speed alone can just reach wrong answers faster
Quality always rises automatically whenever a team works faster
Speed and quality move together, so measuring one is enough
The experiment found no speed gain at all, so time saved is a myth
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 uses the jagged-frontier experiment to show that within the AI's competence people were faster and produced higher quality work, but outside it they finished faster yet were about 19 percent less likely to be correct. Measuring only speed therefore optimizes for getting to bad outcomes sooner, so speed and quality must be tracked together.

questions.question: What cadence does Lesson 26 recommend as a sensible default for a typical organization?
options: Refresh the AI inventory and run evidence checks quarterly, review the full policy annually, and review high-risk systems on the quarterly cycle
Run a full audit once, never again, because AI stays the same after setup
Review everything on an annual basis only, including high-risk systems
Do not schedule audits; run them only when someone remembers to ask
questions.explanation: The lesson recommends, as a sensible default, refreshing the inventory and running evidence checks quarterly, reviewing the full policy annually, and keeping high-risk systems (anything handling client data, money, or regulated information) on the tighter quarterly cycle. It stresses that the operative requirement is a scheduled date, because a check that only happens when someone remembers is not a cadence.

questions.question: Why does shadow AI carry more risk than classic shadow IT, according to Lesson 20?
options: Because AI tools are more expensive than other software
Because shadow AI affects only the marketing and engineering teams
Because AI does not just store your data, it processes it, and in many cases retains it, trains on it, or sends it to a model provider you never reviewed
Because unsanctioned AI is always malicious by intent
questions.explanation: The lesson defines the difference: shadow IT stores or transfers data to unapproved services, while shadow AI actively processes, learns from, and retains enterprise data in ways that create data exfiltration risk the moment the data is sent, before anyone can review it.

questions.question: The lesson flags four clauses to read before signing an AI agreement: output ownership, whether your data trains the model, who pays when the output is wrong or infringes, and model changes. What does an auto-renewal clause add to that list?
options: Auto-renewal guarantees the vendor will keep the price fixed for the life of the agreement

A ninety-day notice combined with a twelve-month auto-renewal term can leave only a three-week window each year to exit, which is a common way organizations get trapped with a tool, so the lesson pushes the notice down toward thirty days and checks for silent price escalation
Auto-renewal is a legal requirement for all enterprise AI contracts and cannot be changed
Auto-renewal shifts liability for infringing outputs from the buyer to the vendor automatically
questions.explanation: Lesson 18 explains that ninety-day notice plus a twelve-month auto-renewal leaves a three-week annual window to actually get out, the most common reason organizations feel trapped. It advises pushing the notice down toward thirty days or moving to month-to-month, and checking for silent price escalation that can compound above the quoted price.

questions.question: Why does Lesson 3 argue that self-reported time savings are unreliable as evidence that AI is paying off?
options: People tend to overestimate how long their tasks take and how much faster a tool makes them, so a survey of enthusiasm measures a feeling rather than a result
GitHub's controlled experiment proved that time-saved claims are always false
Self-reports are only unreliable in technology companies, not in operations
The McKinsey survey showed that time saved is never reallocated to new work
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 cites GitHub's own productivity research and reasoning that individuals are poor judges of how long tasks take, so a survey where people say they feel faster measures a feeling, not a P&L line. It recommends measuring a defined task before and after, throughput over a fixed window, or sampled time use instead.

questions.question: In the FinCo case, MIT CISR found that thorough governance built across all five domains backfired. Why did FinCo's program break the company?
options: Its policy took close to a year to write and was outdated on completion, a low-risk prototype took six months to approve, and frustrated teams went back to unsanctioned tools
The governance was adopted too quickly and with too little involvement from legal and compliance
The company had no AI policy at all, so employees had no rules to follow
The council reviewed every use case but never escalated anything to the executive sponsor
questions.explanation: Lesson 30 recounts the FinCo example from MIT CISR: the enterprise policy took close to a year and was outdated when finished, a low-risk agent prototype took six months to get through review, and employees needed layered sign-offs even to access the firm's own secure platform. The slowdown pushed teams back to unsanctioned tools, so shadow AI spread wider than before. This case motivates minimum viable governance.

questions.question: In the worked example, which problem best matches the kind of thing a quarterly audit catches that a real-time monitor would not?
options: A sudden security alert that triggered instantly during business hours
The firm paying for 24 unused seats on a writing assistant and a sanctioned tool gaining a new charting feature without the inventory or policy being updated
A tool that stopped working entirely and could not be reached by anyone
A vendor shutting down its API with no notice to the organization
questions.explanation: The lesson's worked example found three quiet, unglamorous gaps that no real-time signal had flagged: sixteen paid-but-unused writing-assistant seats, a finance tool whose vendor quietly added charting that was past the inventory and policy, and a coding assistant used by two people the policy did not name. These are the kind of drift a scheduled, evidence-based audit catches, not a live monitor.

questions.question: Priya is a senior accountant who doubts the AI reconciliation tool actually works and asks to see one thing it does that she cannot do faster herself. Which reaction is Priya showing, and what does the lesson prescribe?
options: Fear, so she needs reassurance that her job is safe before any evidence is shown
Skepticism, so she needs a specific, honest demonstration of the tool's real limits rather than a slogan
Fear, so she should be moved to a non-AI role to reduce her distress
Skepticism, so she should be told to trust the rollout plan and stop asking questions
questions.explanation: The lesson separates fear (emotional, worried about losing work or value) from skepticism (rational doubt that the tool works or is worth it). Skepticism answers to evidence, but only evidence that is specific and honest. Mara runs a live reconciliation and shows the tool's actual error, which gives Priya the honest, specific answer her skepticism is asking for.

questions.question: A manager funded a two-week launch campaign and usage climbed during it. When the campaign ended, usage collapsed. What does this pattern most directly indicate?
options: The usage was driven by the launch event, so it was a spike rather than compounding momentum
The adoption is momentum and will resume on its own
The tool only works during high-energy campaigns
The users need more training before they can adopt the tool
questions.explanation: The lesson's test separates the two: a spike depends on the thing that started it and collapses when the event stops, while momentum runs on its own returns. If usage collapses when the launch event ends, what you had was a spike, not momentum.

questions.question: Which set of resilience moves does Lesson 23 describe to manage model and provider dependency risk?
options: Use only one provider, avoid testing alternatives, and sign the shortest possible contract
Rely on the provider's promises and avoid writing anything down

Inventory dependencies, flag single points of failure, test one or two alternatives on a regular schedule, keep work portable, put terms in the contract, and write an exit plan for the few use cases that would hurt most
Procure every tool through a reseller so the risk sits with the reseller
questions.explanation: The lesson's resilience playbook is six moves, each a governance activity: inventory your dependencies, find the single points of failure, test one or two alternatives regularly, keep your work portable, put the terms in the contract (notice before retirement or material price change, and data exportability), and write a one-page exit plan for the few AI use cases where a change or failure would genuinely hurt.

questions.question: A pilot succeeds, yet the use case fails when the company tries to roll it out broadly. According to Lesson 29, which set of conditions explains the most common cause of that failure?
options: The underlying model was never good enough, and the pilot team hid its errors
The pilot depended on curated data, relaxed governance with manual review, and outputs that did not act, and those support beams are removed at scale
The finance team always refuses to fund production deployments regardless of pilot results
Employees in the wider organization are inherently more resistant to change than the pilot team
questions.explanation: The lesson names the three assumptions a pilot leans on: curated data, governance applied after the fact with humans reviewing outputs, and a system that informs rather than acts. At scale those vanish, which is why Gartner finds at least 50% of generative AI projects are abandoned after proof of concept and MIT reports roughly 95% of pilots never reach measurable impact. Model quality is not the cause.

questions.question: Why does Lesson 31 insist that consolidation happen at renewal dates rather than as soon as the decision is made?
options: Because vendors legally cannot be contacted outside a renewal window

Because a forced mid-contract cutover pays twice for the same job and teaches the organization that consolidation is painful, while a renewal date is when ending a contract is cheap and a new one is negotiable
Because employees need at least a year to learn any new tool before switching
Because the lesson recommends waiting until the annual audit to make any decisions
questions.explanation: Lesson 31 describes consolidation as having a natural rhythm: contracts end on dates, and attempting a forced cutover mid-contract means paying twice for the same job, once to the old vendor and once to the new one, which teaches the organization that consolidation is painful. It therefore builds a renewal calendar from the inventory, names a migration owner, archives what must be kept, requests data deletion in writing, and ends the contract before auto-renewal rather than after.

questions.question: According to Lesson 24, when does an AI-generated output get copyright protection in the United States?
options: Whenever a contract states that the customer owns the output
Whenever a vendor trains on the customer's data
Only where a human author has determined sufficient expressive elements of the output, such as through substantial editing, arrangement, or a human-authored work perceptible in the result
Whenever the output is generated by an enterprise AI tool
questions.explanation: The lesson is built on the human authorship requirement: copyright protects only material that is the product of human creativity, and a prompt alone does not make you the author. A work can be protected where a human determines sufficient expressive elements, for example by arranging, editing, or modifying the output so human expression is perceptible. A contract that says you own an output cannot create a copyright that the law does not recognize.

questions.question: An adoption owner is deciding whether to report a failed month-end test in the internal newsletter. Which reasoning matches the lesson's position on reporting setbacks?
options: Conceal the setback until a positive result can be reported to avoid spooking the workforce
Report the setback only to the executive team and keep the wider staff on the wins
Report the setback in the same forum and on the same schedule as wins, with the specific lesson learned and the next step
Mention the setback once without numbers so nobody can question it
questions.explanation: The lesson prescribes that wins and setbacks appear in the same recurring forum on the same schedule, and that a setback is reported with what was learned and what is next rather than as bare bad news. Concealment undermines trust because employees already know AI is powerful, so a hidden setback reads as a leader withholding the whole story.

questions.question: In the worked example, Vendor A won the demo but scored 54 while Vendor B scored 84 on the pre-set rubric. Why did Vendor B win even though it was less impressive in the demo?
options: Because Vendor B was cheaper per seat even though its license was higher
Because Vendor B's capability score of 3 beat Vendor A's score of 5 on weighted terms
Because the firm weighted data handling and oversight heaviest, and Vendor B was the one the firm could actually govern, with a usable exit path, while Vendor A failed on data handling and exit
Because the reveal order of the demo influenced the final decision more than the rubric
questions.explanation: The rubric weighted data handling (5) and security and oversight (5 and 4) most heavily, because the firm's policy flagged those as top risks. Vendor B won on data handling, oversight, and exit path. Vendor A's capability edge (5 vs 3) could not outweigh a data-handling failure and a non-existent exit path, which is exactly why the rubric is set before looking.

questions.question: An adoption owner is picking champions for a company AI rollout and is tempted to choose the three loudest volunteers. Based on the lesson, what is the most important correction to that approach?
options: Choose people primarily by their technical skill with the tool
Choose people with existing influence in each department and check bandwidth, because influence and available time are what actually move adoption
Pick only people from departments that already support the AI rollout
Pick as many volunteers as possible so no department is left out, regardless of their role
questions.explanation: The lesson warns that the loudest volunteer is not always the most influential person, and influence is the trait that moves adoption. It also stresses representation across the whole organization and checking bandwidth so champions have time to help. Selecting for influence and time, not enthusiasm or technical skill alone, makes the network work.

questions.question: Lesson 13 argues that surveys and self-reports routinely overstate AI use. Which of these is one of the mechanisms the lesson names for why what people say runs ahead of what they do?
options: Social desirability: people give the answer they think leadership wants, especially about an approved initiative
Users always answer surveys on a Friday when they are most productive
Self-reports are always accurate but the data is slow to arrive
The only bias is that people underreport their use out of modesty
questions.explanation: Lesson 13 identifies social desirability, recalling a feeling as a fact (the same self-report problem as the time-saved metric in Lesson 3), and the observer's incentive as three mechanisms that push self-reported usage ahead of real usage. People answer questions the way they think they should, especially when leadership has declared the initiative important.

questions.question: Priya's firm trained everyone and reached 94 percent completion, but only about a third kept using AI in their work. What best represents her fix, according to the lesson?
options: Schedule another round of all-hands workshops to repeat the original training
Blame the staff for low motivation and require them to retake the module
Stop measuring completions, build a spaced reinforcement cadence, and turn her power users into champions who deliver reusable local training
Measure completions more often so the report shows higher engagement
questions.explanation: Priya reads the gap between completion and behaviour as the transfer gap, not a staff failure. Her fix is the scalable division of labor: reusable material written once, spaced reinforcement that repeats the skill in the flow of work, and champions who deliver local training for their own teams. This replaces the one-time event and reflects the principle that the behaviour, not the completion count, is what the training investment buys.

questions.question: Lesson 14 opens by arguing that telling the team to review every piece of AI output is the most common oversight mistake. Why does the blanket 'review everything' instruction fail?
options: Because it makes people review less often out of defiance
Because it covers everything without sorting what matters, so attention flattens and the outputs that genuinely need care get the same glance as the rest
Because it is too hard for most employees to remember
Because reviewing every output slows the system down past the point of usefulness
questions.explanation: Lesson 14 explains that when every output is a mandatory review, the reviews blur and stop being decisions, so the outputs that genuinely need care get exactly the same attention as the ones that do not. The fix is a supervision bar that sorts AI work into categories and names the ones that require a real, owned human decision.

questions.question: A stakeholder proposes 'share of employees who used AI this month' as the program's north-star metric. Why does this make a poor north-star, per the lesson?
options: It is too hard to measure reliably, so leadership will not trust it
It is a vanity metric that describes activity without describing value, so it can climb while the organization is no better off
It is a lagging indicator that only reports what already happened last month
It is not financially material enough to justify a budget request
questions.explanation: The lesson classifies the share of people using AI as a vanity metric, along with prompt counts and active-user counts. Such a metric scores activity, not value, and can rise while no real work improves. You may track it, but it should not be the north-star seat.

questions.question: A pilot reported a strong win in March but could not scale in June, and the March claim is still on the internal board. What does the lesson identify as the correct action?
options: Leave the March claim up because it was accurate when it was made
Quietly remove the March number so nobody questions the program
Update the stale claim on a schedule, revalidate it, and correct it publicly with the current result
Issue a larger corrective announcement admitting the whole program is failing
questions.explanation: The lesson warns that the biggest source of AI-washing-adjacent damage is not new lies but old claims left standing after the situation changes, and prescribes a review where every published claim gets revalidated or corrected. Retiring a stale claim is cheaper and more trust-preserving than defending it later.

questions.question: Lesson 14 defines three ways humans relate to an AI system. Which configuration is the right fit for an irreversible, high-consequence decision such as final customer pricing?
options: Human-in-the-loop: a named person must approve the output before the workflow proceeds
Human-on-the-loop: the system runs and a person supervises from above, stepping in only on anomalies
Human-in-command only, with no daily involvement at all
No human involvement, because the system's accuracy makes review unnecessary
questions.explanation: Lesson 14 sets the bar by consequence and reversibility. High-consequence or hard-to-reverse work sits below the bar and needs human-in-the-loop: a named person must sign off before release. Human-on-the-loop fits routine, reversible, low-impact work where catching the occasional anomaly is enough.

questions.question: In the worked example, Priya's network keeps adoption numbers climbing even after she is reassigned to another project for six weeks. What best explains that outcome?
options: The AI tool became so reliable that nobody needed support
Priya's north-star metric was set too low to matter
The champions were tied to the way of working rather than to the launch, and had the time, structure, and recognition to keep playing their rhythm without her
The company stopped requiring coordinators to use the tool
questions.explanation: Priya selected champions by influence and bandwidth, gave them a monthly circle, a defined support role, and an ongoing post-launch job. Because the support role belonged to the champions, not to Priya, the network carried adoption when she was pulled away. This reflects the lesson's core point that the support role outlives any single owner.

questions.question: Lesson 27 recommends start with showback and graduate to chargeback. What is the reason for that order?
options: Chargeback is more expensive to operate, so it should be saved for later
Showback creates direct financial penalty first, then chargeback adds visibility
Roughly 90% tagging coverage is required before a chargeback model can be applied fairly, so organizations build reliable attribution under showback first to avoid disputes
Chargeback is illegal until a company reaches a minimum size
questions.explanation: Lesson 27, drawing on the MLflow guide, explains that roughly 90% tagging coverage is required before a chargeback model can be applied fairly, and that below that threshold untagged costs create disputes and erode trust. So most organizations start with showback, which builds awareness through transparency without moving money, then move to chargeback once tagging is reliable.

questions.question: Why does Lesson 18 warn that a standard SaaS vendor template is a trap when applied to AI procurement?
options: Because AI contracts are always shorter and therefore missing necessary legal boilerplate

Because AI tools break the assumptions SaaS templates were built on: the output is probabilistic, the model can change under you, the vendor may train on your data by default, and output IP may not be protectable, all of which standard templates do not address
Because SaaS templates are too expensive to customize for AI buying
Because standard templates never include any pricing terms
questions.explanation: Lesson 18 states that a classic SaaS product was deterministic, predictable software, but AI is probabilistic, can change under you, and the vendor can alter or remove the model on short notice. Standard templates were not built for these characteristics, which is why the license has to cover output ownership, training-data defaults, who answers for wrong or infringing output, and model deprecation.

questions.question: The lesson lays an AI ROI case out in four layers so a CFO can read it. Which description matches that structure?
options: Financial outcomes on top, then operational metrics, then behavioural metrics, then AI-specific health, with each layer feeding the one above it
AI-specific health on top, with financial outcomes at the base so usage is highlighted
Four separate reports with no connection between layers
A single headline ROI number with no supporting evidence
questions.explanation: Lesson 28 structures the proof as financial outcomes on top, operational metrics beneath, behavioural metrics next, and AI-specific health at the base, each layer feeding the one above it. The top layer carries the dollars and is the only one the board reads on its own, and the bottom three exist to defend it.

questions.question: Lesson 27 explains that traditional SaaS budgeting habits break down for AI because of a structural difference. What is it?
options: AI software always costs more per user than traditional software
A large share of AI spend is usage-driven: it scales with adoption and spikes when a workflow succeeds, so it is structurally hard to forecast
AI vendors refuse to publish their prices
AI budgets are always owned by a single clean function, unlike traditional software
questions.explanation: Lesson 27 states that a large share of AI spend is usage-driven rather than seat-driven, that it scales with and often spikes when a workflow works, and that it is owned by no single function, which makes it structurally hard to forecast. The lesson describes an automation that costs nothing until it works, then costs more every month as people route work to it.

questions.question: Lesson 19 warns against spreading responsibility across security, IT, legal, and the business team until everyone is 'loosely responsible.' What does the governance practice the lesson cites argue instead?
options: That a committee of all those teams should approve every low-risk internal tool

That shared input is useful but is not shared accountability, so each AI use case needs one named accountable owner, with an independent challenge that reviews the risk rather than relying on the person who is most excited about the tool
That the CISO should personally own every technology, legal, employee, and business consequence of AI
That the vendor's contract should be treated as the accountable owner since it names the liabilities
questions.explanation: Lesson 19 quotes the AI risk governance practice: shared input is not shared accountability, and when accountability is split, difficult decisions tend to wait. So each use case gets one named accountable owner, and the person promoting the use case should not be the only one deciding its risk is acceptable, which is why an independent challenge or governance committee reviews the decision. The vendor contract is explicitly called 'a piece of paper,' not an owner.

questions.question: An organization builds its entitlement groups as a department group containing team groups, assigns the license to the department group, and finds that part of the department never received access. What does Lesson 32 identify as the cause and the fix?
options: The license count was too low for the group, so the fix is to buy more seats than the group contains
SCIM had not been enabled, so the fix is to turn on directory sync and wait for propagation
When a license is applied to a nested group only the immediate first-level user members receive it, so entitlement groups should be kept flat and the nesting left to the directory elsewhere
Direct assignments had already been made to those users, so the fix is to clear every direct assignment in the tenant
questions.explanation: Lesson 32 lists nested groups as the first of four provisioning edges, citing the documented behavior that applying a license to a nested group licenses only immediate first-level user members. The recommended fix is flat entitlement groups, one per job category, with nesting handled elsewhere. The other options misidentify the mechanism: group licensing already requires a license for each unique member, SCIM is not the cause of the nesting limit, and direct assignments are a separate edge.

questions.question: Dhara's worked example relies on several guardrail families working together. Which combination best describes how she keeps an expensive failure from escaping?
options: She only restricts the agent's speed so it cannot act too quickly
She relies entirely on the model's accuracy to stay in its lane

Scope defines the agent's lane, permissions deny everything outside it, reversibility routes expensive-to-reverse actions to a named human, observability logs every action, and containment blocks out-of-lane tool calls
She assigns every action a watchful person and keeps the agent offline
questions.explanation: Lesson 25 shows Dhara building all five families: scope limits the agent to the support inbox and refund tool, permissions deny everything else by default, reversibility escalates expensive-to-reverse actions to a named support lead, observability logs every action, and containment blocks calls outside the allowlist. The lesson states that every affected action should have three things: a guardrail that stops it, a log that records it, and a person who owns the outcome.

questions.question: A manager wants high long-term retention of an AI skill across the whole firm. Which training design best reflects the evidence in the lesson?
options: Run one intensive full-day workshop so everyone learns it together once
Replace the single session with short re-engagements repeated on a regular cadence, such as a weekly practice prompt tied to real work
Deliver a longer version of the single workshop to make it more thorough
Make the one-time module mandatory and require completion by the end of the week
questions.explanation: The lesson cites research on spaced versus massed training: spaced training, with long intervals between sessions, leads to more robust memory than massed training, which piles everything into one sitting. The one-time workshop is the massed approach and most likely to fade. Short re-engagements on a fixed cadence (spaced reinforcement) transfer better than a single event.

questions.question: Which practice does Lesson 24 recommend for a non-technical owner to protect the organization's data and outputs?
options: Assume enterprise tools never train on data, and paste AI output unchanged to save time
Register every AI output as-is with the copyright office without disclosing AI use

Find and verify the data-use clause before routing sensitive data through a tool, classify confidential data by the color rule, require real human authorship for load-bearing outputs, assign rights from contractors in writing, and keep a record of the human contribution
Avoid using AI for any content a customer could see
questions.explanation: The lesson's practical moves are: find the data-use clause before you sign and confirm in writing that the vendor does not train without consent, route sensitive data using the red, yellow, green color rule, decide which outputs are load-bearing and require genuine human authorship for those, tell employees the difference between pasted output and authored work, assign contractor rights in writing, and preserve drafts that show the human contribution. Verification matters because the protections vary by vendor and must be checked in the actual contract, not assumed from marketing.

questions.question: A leader plans to treat the first 30 days of an AI rollout as the entire change effort. What does the habit-formation research cited in the lesson say about that plan?
options: A 30-day window is sufficient because workplace change is more structured than a daily personal habit
A habit reliably forms in 21 days for most people, so 30 days is generous
The median time to automaticity was 66 days with a range of 18 to 254 days, and even that describes a selected group, so a month is too short
Most participants in the study formed habits within 30 days, so the plan is reasonable
questions.explanation: The lesson grounds the '30-day on-ramp is too short' thesis in the Lally study: a median of 66 days to reach the modeled automaticity plateau, a range of 18 to 254 days, and even that figure describes a selected subset of motivated volunteers. A month is the beginning of the change effort, not the end.

questions.question: Lesson 20 argues that banning shadow AI makes the problem worse. What is the evidence for this?
options: Blocking an application eliminates its use because employees respect the restriction
45% of workers find a workaround when an application is blocked, pushing usage underground and past the few visibility signals you had
Banning is effective because unapproved tools simply disappear from the network
Judging employees is the correct response because shadow AI is only a discipline problem
questions.explanation: The lesson cites UpGuard's finding that 45% of workers find a workaround when an application is blocked, so prohibition compromises visibility rather than eliminating usage. Treating it as a discipline problem is contradicted by the finding that security leadership itself uses unapproved tools at similar rates.

questions.question: Lesson 17 argues that evaluating an AI tool is a risk decision, not a shopping trip. What best captures why the two are different?
options: Because shopping trips are faster, while risk decisions require a budget meeting

Because when you compare products you are judging flash, but when you adopt a tool you take on a risk profile, a data flow, a support relationship, and a bundle of obligations that outlive the contract
Because risk decisions always reject every vendor, while shopping trips always approve one
Because product comparison is done by IT, while risk decisions belong to legal
questions.explanation: Lesson 17 states the trap directly: comparing one product against another judges the products, while adopting a tool adopts its risk profile, data flow, support relationship, and obligations that outlive the contract. Those are different comparisons, and the second one governs.

questions.question: Mateo wants to grow adoption past the novelty dip. Which action best reflects the lesson's guidance to build breadth through depth?
options: Launch an org-wide push so every department tries the tool at least once
Broaden the tool license to the largest department first, even though it has no ready-made AI workflow
Find the adjacent workflow for the people already using the tool deeply and expand the tool into that workflow with the same users first
Reward any team that mentions AI in a meeting with a public shoutout
questions.explanation: The lesson says the people already using AI for one part of their job are the cheapest place to get the next win, so expansion should start with the next adjacent workflow for existing users. Breadth through depth, not depth through breadth. This mirrors Mateo bringing the billing team in after the password-reset win, rather than chasing the marketing department with no ready-made workflow.

questions.question: Two invoice specialists quietly went back to typing invoices by hand. Which action did Lucia take that most directly removed the friction driving their fallback?
options: She published the time-saved numbers in the weekly all-hands to prove the new way works
She expanded the tool to the load-confirmation workflow so the same team used it for more of their day
She changed the tool's settings so the confirmation prompt only appears when the tool's confidence is low, instead of on every invoice
She updated the standard operating procedure to make the AI-assisted workflow the documented default
questions.explanation: When Lucia asked the two specialists what pushed them back, they said the tool asked for a confirmation on every invoice and it felt like a nag. She removed that friction by making the confirmation appear only at low confidence. The other options are the short-term win, consolidation, and anchoring steps, which are real but not the friction fix.

questions.question: The lesson explains how the GDPR restricts automated decisions about people. A tool that screens job applicants and surfaces a shortlist that a recruiter simply stamps with approval is best understood as what?
options: A form of automated decision-making under Article 22, because a person can still contest the recruiter's approval, so there is no issue
Not regulated, because the recruiter always reviews the list before acting
A decision based solely on automated processing with a legal or similarly significant effect, which the GDPR restricts and requires safeguards for, including a genuine human route to overturn it
Compliant by default because employment decisions about applicants are exempt from privacy law
questions.explanation: Lesson 21 explains Article 22's right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, that produces legal or similarly significant effects. The regulator's guidance gives e-recruiting with no human review as an example. The lesson's working rule when a model produces a decision a person will feel is to route it through a human who can actually overturn it, not just stamp it. A recruiter who merely stamps the tool's shortlist does not satisfy the human-in-the-loop safeguard, and employment is not exempt from these rules.

questions.question: According to the McKinsey survey cited in Lesson 1, which finding most directly supports the case that an adoption owner's job is a program, not a rollout?
options: 70 percent of employees personally feel ready for AI while only 27 percent of leaders believe their organizations are ready to change around it
Employees are less ready for AI than their organizations are
Individual readiness accounts for 48 percent of value capture, nearly twice the share of organizational readiness
Treating AI as a technology deployment reliably captures the most enterprise value
questions.explanation: Lesson 1 cites McKinsey's survey: 70 percent of employees feel personally ready while only 27 percent of leaders believe their organizations are ready, and organizational readiness (48 percent) matters nearly twice as much as personal readiness (25 percent). This shows the value comes from ongoing organizational change, which is the program.

questions.question: In the four-track adoption audit, which track is the one that captures the data flowing into AI tools, such as the recruiting coordinator pasting candidate resumes into a free consumer tool?
options: The tool track, which lists every AI tool in use
The workflow track, which maps which jobs and steps use AI
The perception track, which compares leader estimates to worker reports
The data track, which records what information is entered or uploaded into the tools
questions.explanation: The lesson defines the data track as recording what kinds of information are typed, pasted, or uploaded into these tools, the risk surface that a future data policy and incident response will need to account for. The candidate-resume example is presented as a data-track finding.

questions.question: Lesson 30 argues that the question which separates real AI governance from theater is most fundamentally:
options: When an AI model does something it should not do, who has the authority to stop it, and does that person answer to someone who does not depend on the deployment succeeding
How many dashboards and model registries the organization has built to monitor its AI systems
Whether the AI council has a lawyers and a security officer in the room
How many policies the organization has written about responsible AI use
questions.explanation: Lesson 30 builds on the MIT Sloan Management Review argument that governance is theater when nobody can hit the stop button. The load-bearing question is who can actually stop a misbehaving model and whether that person has the standing to do it without reporting to someone who benefits from the 'yes'. Registries, dashboards, and policies are visibility infrastructure, not accountability.

questions.question: In Lesson 13's worked example, Amara builds a feedback loop. What is the key move that turns her collected usage data into a loop rather than a data dump?
options: Running a larger, more frequent survey to confirm what people say
Closing the loop: making a visible change from the behavioral signals, such as fixing the reply-length friction, and telling people what she changed and why
Holding more department meetings so everyone can state their enthusiasm
Buying a better analytics dashboard and watching it without acting
questions.explanation: Lesson 13 defines closing the loop as taking what the signals say, making a decision, and feeding that decision back so users see their behavior shaped the program. Amara moves the reply-length task to need less fixing and tells both teams what the usage data showed. Collecting information that never changes anything is data hoarding, not feedback.

questions.question: Your team uses an AI drafting tool, and you want to reduce the number of users who quit after one bad answer. Which action best reflects recovery done before the first failure?
options: Wait for failures to happen, then apologize for each one and promise the tool will do better
Calibrate expectations in training: tell users what the tool is good at, where it confidently invents, and the cheap check that catches a bad output in seconds
Hide the tool's limitations so users trust it more
Require everyone to accept the tool's output without reviewing it
questions.explanation: The lesson's calibration section says most bad first experiences are caused by a wrong expectation, not a broken tool. Telling people before first use what the tool handles well, where it guesses, and how to run a cheap check turns a bad answer from a verdict on the idea into an expected risk the user can manage.

questions.question: Nora's one-page policy in the worked example names a quarterly review rhythm and an approved-tool list that any new tool must join before use. Which of Tenable's five pillars does that set of lines serve?
options: Scope and roles only
The governance and change process, which keeps the approved list current and gives employees a visible way to request a new tool
Data handling only, because it only concerns what data enters tools
Enforcement and acknowledgment, because it concerns sign-offs only
questions.explanation: Lesson 15 explains that the approved list only works if there is a governance and change process behind it: a defined way for employees to request a review of a new tool and a decision path that evaluates security, privacy, vendor stability, and data residency. Nora's quarterly review rhythm and the visible request channel are exactly that pillar, and it is what stops her policy from going stale.

questions.question: Lesson 15 lists three reasons most AI policies fail in practice. Which one is specifically about the person who owns the policy?
options: The policy is written in legal jargon so nobody reads it
The policy becomes stale as the AI tool landscape changes
The policy has no real owner who keeps it current, answers the 'is this allowed' question, and handles violations
The policy is too short to cover every possible tool
questions.explanation: Lesson 15 names a policy without a real owner as the third and most relevant failure: it lives in a folder, is signed once, and is forgotten, with nobody tasked to keep it current, answer questions, or respond to violations. The adoption owner's job is to be that person, which is why the pillar calls for naming a single owner rather than a committee.

questions.question: Your support-automation pilot clears its technical checkpoints and early adoption signals. Per the four-phase pathway in Lesson 29, what is the correct next step and the gate it must clear?
options: Skip straight to full-scale rollout everywhere, because a successful pilot is proof the use case will scale

Enter an MVP phase with limited but live exposure and a gate asking whether the solution is safe and stable, whether users adopt it in a real workflow, and whether measurable operational and financial impact justifies scaling
Abandon the pilot and start a new one in a different department to test for repeatability
Move to full scale only after the vendor demonstrates better model accuracy in a benchmark
questions.explanation: The phase order is pilot, MVP, initial scaling, then full scale. The MVP puts the solution into real workflows with limited live exposure, and the decision gates ask whether the model is safe and stable, whether adoption is happening in real workflows, and whether impact justifies scaling. The lesson warns that a pilot is proof, not scale.

questions.question: Lesson 2 gives five tests for whether a workflow is ready for AI. Which profile best describes work where AI is most likely to create value?
options: High volume, predictable inputs, a clear checkable output, cheap errors, and repeatable steps
Rare, high-stakes judgment calls where a wrong answer is hard to detect and expensive to fix
Open-ended creative work that is the organization's differentiator and has no objective ground truth
Any work where people are enthusiastic about the tool, regardless of volume or structure
questions.explanation: Lesson 2 defines value-ready work as having structured, repeatable inputs; a clear output someone consumes; an output that can be checked cheaply; errors that are cheap to fix; and enough volume that gains accumulate. Rare, high-stakes judgment calls and open-ended creative work fail several of those tests.
